$why: THE SEEDED-FAULT CATALOGUE — how QAAI finds out whether it finds anything.
QAAI has never been able to say "we detect N% of seeded defects", which is the
ground truth every coverage claim rests on: a 90% coverage number over a suite
that catches nothing is worth less than a 40% number over a suite that catches
everything, and until this file existed the product could not tell those two
apart about ITSELF.
Each entry is one defect, individually switchable, with a machine-readable
record of what it breaks and which declared surface item it lives on. The
harness (packages/cli/src/bench.ts) switches one on, runs the suite, records
DETECTED / MISSED / NOT_EXERCISED, switches it off, and repeats.
── WHY SOURCE PATCHES AND NOT A RUNTIME FLAG ───────────────────────────────
A fault is a set of `find`/`replace` edits against real lines of the demo app,
applied on disk and reverted byte-for-byte. Three reasons, in order of how much
they matter:
1. IT IS THE REAL THING. A flag-guarded branch is a branch the app always
carries; a patched line is the defect a developer would actually have
written. DEMO_PLANTED_BUG is the flag version and it has one defect in it,
for ever, because adding a second would mean another env var and another
permanent branch.
2. IMPOSSIBLE TO LEAVE ON. The clean baseline is asserted STRUCTURALLY and not
against a digest committed in this file: every edit's `find` text must be
present exactly once and its `replace` text must be absent, which is
precisely the statement "no fault from this catalogue is applied right
now". It is checked BEFORE the first fault and AFTER the last, together
with a per-file digest taken at the start of the run and compared at the
end. A digest committed here would have been stronger and wrong: it goes
stale on any unrelated edit to the demo app, and a benchmark that is red
for a reason unconnected to the benchmark is a benchmark somebody
switches off.
3. NO NEW ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE. A connector's switches belong on a row the
customer owns, and a benchmark's switches belong in the benchmark.
The cost is that an edit to the demo app can invalidate an anchor. That is a
FEATURE here: the patch stops applying, the bench reports the fault as
NOT_APPLICABLE with the file and the anchor named, and the count of faults it
could not attempt is printed beside the detection rate rather than quietly
shrinking it.
── THE RATE IS PER CLASS, NEVER BLENDED ────────────────────────────────────
"We catch 90% of broken validations and 20% of silent failures" is a finding a
team acts on. One blended percentage is a marketing number, and it is also
unstable: it moves when somebody adds three more faults of the class we happen
to be good at. `class` is what the rate is grouped by, and a class with one
member reports n=1 rather than hiding behind the average.
A fault whose surface no test ever touched proves nothing about the assertions.
It is a COVERAGE gap, and reporting it as MISSED would blame the assertions for
it while reporting it as DETECTED would be fiction. It is excluded from both
halves of the fraction and counted beside it. A benchmark that cannot tell "we
had no test" from "our test passed anyway" is useless in both directions.

$classes.WRONG_TOTAL: A number the user reads is arithmetically wrong while every other number on the page stays right. Only an assertion about MEANING catches it; a pixel diff and a 200-check both sail past.
$classes.BROKEN_VALIDATION: A constraint the form declares is no longer enforced on the server. Caught only by a test that submits the invalid case, which is the half of testing most suites do not have.
$classes.SERVER_ERROR: A path that answered 404 or 200 now throws. The easiest class to catch and therefore the floor: a suite that misses these is not reaching the path at all.
$classes.A11Y: An accessible name or a label association disappears. Caught only by a test type most suites do not run, which is why this class and the per-TYPE coverage breakdown are read together.
$classes.OFF_BY_ONE: A boundary moves by one. The demo has no pagination, so these are the free-shipping threshold and the stock clamp — the same defect shape as an off-by-one page size, on the boundaries this application actually has.
$classes.SILENT_FAILURE: The user-visible flow succeeds and a side effect does not happen. Nothing errors, nothing is red, and the only witness is an assertion about the side effect itself.
$classes.SECURITY: A guard against an attacker-controlled input is removed. The response is a 303 either way, so a status-code assertion cannot see it.
$classes.FLAKY_RACE: Intermittent. The point of the class is that a single run cannot settle it, so the bench reports the repetition count and the share of repetitions that went red — never one boolean.

faults.title: Tax truncates instead of rounding
faults.breaks: Every order total is up to one cent low. Subtotal, shipping and the per-line prices stay correct and the tax line itself is off by at most a cent — small enough that a human reviewing the page will not see it, and large enough that a test comparing total against subtotal + shipping + tax will.

faults.title: The order total omits shipping
faults.breaks: The totals block still prints a shipping line with the right figure and the grand total no longer includes it. Two numbers on one page that disagree — the same shape as the planted bug, on a different addend, so this class has two members and its rate is not an n of one.

faults.title: Checkout no longer requires a card number
faults.breaks: POST /checkout accepts an order with no card number and redirects to the confirmation page. The markup still says `required`, so a browser blocks it and curl does not — which is why a server-side negative test is the only thing that can see this.

faults.title: An unknown product id throws instead of 404ing
faults.breaks: GET /products/does-not-exist reads a property off undefined and answers 500 with Express's default error page. The 404 branch is gone.

edits.replace:
const product = findProduct(req.params.id);
  if (false as boolean) {

faults.editNote: `if (false as boolean)` rather than deleting the block, because a fault must change BEHAVIOUR and not shape: deleting it would also delete the lines, and a diff that moves everything below it is a diff nobody can review. The cast is what stops TypeScript narrowing the branch away and reporting the body as unreachable.

faults.title: The checkout email field loses its label association
faults.breaks: The input keeps its id, its type and its `required`, and has no accessible name. axe reports a label violation; every functional test still passes, because `fill('#email')` does not care whether the field is labelled.

edits.find:
<label for="email">Email address</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" value="${esc(email)}" required autocomplete="email">
edits.replace: Email address

faults.editNote: A `<span>` and not a deletion. Deleting the text would also remove the visible prompt, and a screenshot diff would then catch this for the wrong reason — the fault would be reported DETECTED by a test that noticed the layout, not the accessibility. As written the field still reads as labelled to a human and is unlabelled to an API, which is the defect accessibility testing exists to find.

faults.title: Free shipping needs one cent more than the threshold
faults.breaks: A subtotal of exactly $150.00 is charged $7.00 shipping and $150.01 is not. The home page advertises "over $150" and the code said at-or-above, so only a test sitting exactly ON the boundary can tell the difference.

faults.title: The cart accepts one more than the stock
faults.breaks: Adding 99 of the grinder (stock 5) lands 6 in the cart instead of 5. The order goes through and the inventory table on /admin still says 5.

edits.find: else lines.push({ productId, quantity: Math.min(product.stock, quantity) });
edits.replace: else lines.push({ productId, quantity: Math.min(product.stock + 1, quantity) });

faults.title: The order receipt is never sent
faults.breaks: The order is created, the confirmation page says a receipt is on its way to the customer, and no mail is sent. No error, no log line, no red test — unless something asserts on the mailbox. This is the class of defect that reaches production and is found by a customer.
faults.editNote: The same `if (false as boolean)` guard as FAULT-500, and for an additional reason here: every identifier inside the call — `email`, `order`, `formatMoney` — stays referenced, so the patched file has no unused-variable error and the fault is a behaviour change and nothing else. Commenting the block out instead would have removed four live references and turned one seeded defect into a compile error.

faults.title: The sign-in redirect honours an absolute URL
faults.breaks: POST /login with next=https://evil.example sends the freshly authenticated user there. The response is a 303 with or without the fault and the only difference is the Location header, so a test asserting "signing in lands me somewhere" passes and one asserting WHERE does not.

faults.title: Roughly a quarter of sessions are re-minted on every request
faults.breaks: A session whose uuid starts with 0-3 gets a brand new id on every request, so its cart empties between pages. Consistent for an unlucky session and intermittent across runs, which is what a session flake actually looks like from a test's point of view.
faults.nondeterminismNote: NOT REPRODUCIBLE FROM THE BENCH SEED, said out loud rather than implied. The draw is `randomUUID()` inside the demo app, which the bench does not control and will not reach into: a fault that needed the application rewired to be measurable would stop being the defect it is modelling. So the bench runs it `repetitions` times, reports the share of repetitions that went red, and carries a caveat naming this fault as the reason the run is not bit-reproducible from its seed.
